title: A Spectral-Grassmann Wasserstein metric for operator representations of dynamical systems
claim: Standard operator distances respond erratically or inconsistently to controlled system shifts, while ours varies smoothly, monotonically, and stays invariant to sampling frequency.
layout: 4 line-plot panels in one row, shared legend on top, shared y-axis
description: A single row of four line plots sharing a legend across the top. The legend lists six similarity measures by color: Hilbert-Schmidt (orange), Operator (purple), Martin (gray), SOT (green), GOT (red), and SGOT with eta=0.5 (blue). Panels (a) to (c) plot normalized metric value from 0 to 1 against frequency in Hz, decay rate, and operator rank. Each panel shows how the metrics change as one property of a linear oscillator is shifted. Metrics dip to zero at the reference value. The gray Martin curve is noisy. Orange and purple curves plateau in (a). Green and red curves saturate quickly in (b) and (c). The blue SGOT curve is nearly linear and smooth. Panel (d) plots unnormalized metric value against sampling frequency in Hz. Hilbert-Schmidt, Operator and Martin vary strongly, while SGOT stays flat and low near zero. The eye goes first to the blue line and the colored curves.
caption: Similarity measures' behaviors under four scenarios of shifts of a linear oscillatory system: (a) frequency shift, (b) decay rate shift, (c) operator rank/subspace shift, (d) sampling frequency variation. In scenarios (a,b,c), metric values are normalized by their maximum.
abstract: The geometry of dynamical systems estimated from trajectory data is a major challenge for machine learning applications. Koopman and transfer operators provide a linear representation of nonlinear dynamics through their spectral decomposition, offering a natural framework for comparison. We propose a novel approach representing each system as a distribution of its joint operator eigenvalues and spectral projectors and defining a metric between systems leveraging optimal transport. The proposed metric is invariant to the sampling frequency of trajectories. It is also computationally efficient, supported by finite-sample convergence guarantees, and enables the computation of FrÃ©chet means, providing interpolation between dynamical systems. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show that our approach consistently outperforms standard operator-based distances in machine learning applications, including dimensionality reduction and classification, and provides meaningful interpolation between dynamical systems.
